newsitem.title: USA: Dole tax plan takes spotlight in Mass. Senate debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole tax plan takes spotlight in Mass. Senate debate.

text.p: Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole's plan to cut taxes took the spotlight Tuesday in the sixth debate for the Senate seat from Massachusetts.

Democratic incumbent Sen. John Kerry, in a statistical dead heat with Republican challenger Gov. William Weld, said 75 percent of Dole's tax cut would reward the two wealthiest men on the stage -- the two millionaire politicians.
Only 25 percent of the more than $500 billion cut in taxes would go to ordinary people like the seven undecided Massachusetts voters who asked the Senate hopefuls questions, he said.
"Republican tax cuts go to the wealthy and I want you to get the tax breaks," Kerry told the citizens panel.
Weld, in his second four-year term, said the Massachusetts economy was languishing when he took office, but since has shed its "Taxachusetts" nickname under his own tax cuts.
"Do you seriously think that things are better off in Massachusetts six years later and 15 tax cuts later?" Weld asked.
"The governor hasn't given you 15 tax cuts. His tax cuts haven't gone to you. My tax cuts will go to you," Kerry responded, pointing to the governor.

Except for an opening question on reports of federal officials ignoring drug shipments from Central America into the United States, the the debate, held at Stonehill College in the Cape Cod town of Eastham, was much like their previous five encounters.

Weld, a former U.S. attorney, said the reports sounded like a "nutty conspiracy," but Kerry said the Justice Department ignored his own warnings in the mid-1980s that the Central Intelligence Agency knew of drug shipments into the United States.
Kerry repeatedly pointed his finger toward the governor but the hour-long debate rarely turned contentious.

Kerry consistently tried to paint Weld as a footsoldier for Dole, citing his support for federal cuts to Medicare and student loans, while Weld portrayed the Democratic senator as out of step with voters on crime and term limits.
